My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near current market price levels and gradually tilting higher. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 181.5 is essentially anchored to wherever the asset was trading at the time of the forecast, with only minor expected movement given typical daily volatility. The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the time horizon lengthens, which reflects the well-established principle that uncertainty compounds over time. At one week, that expands to a range of about 25 points, reflecting the accumulation of daily volatility over several sessions and the possibility of a meaningful macro or company-specific news event intervening. Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a credit event, or a sudden spike in volatility could easily push prices below the lower bound of the one-month range. Geopolitical shocks or a sudden shift in central bank policy rhetoric could have similarly outsized effects. On the upside, a strong earnings beat, an unexpected policy easing signal, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices well above the upper bound. Tail risks in either direction are inherently underrepresented in confidence intervals built around normal volatility assumptions, and actual market behavior in stress scenarios frequently exceeds what historical volatility would suggest.
